profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a market-intelligence software company that sells sentiment and attention-risk dashboards to hedge funds and corporate strategy teams. The analytics team has flagged that the platform’s new 'persistence risk' alert is suddenly overfiring on social-discussion streams about meme stocks and consumer brands. The alert was designed to distinguish true long-range dependence in customer attention from short-memory imitation effects that only look persistent. Context: after a recent model update, several clients complained that the dashboard labels ordinary hype cycles as structurally persistent. Agenda: review why the alert is misclassifying bursty behavioral data, diagnose whether the issue comes from the test logic, the simulation benchmark, or the interpretation layer, and decide on a corrective action that can be shipped before the next client review. Expected outcome: both participants believe they have agreed on a quick validation plan and a near-term fix, but they retain subtle differences about what exactly is being tested, what evidence counts as a confirmed diagnosis, and what part of the pipeline the fix covers.

members.name: Elena Park
members.expertise: Behavioral signal interpretation, dashboard metrics, client-facing model validation
members.background: Elena came from a fintech research vendor where she translated quantitative signals into portfolio and communications dashboards for non-technical clients. She now owns the business interpretation of persistence-related alerts and works closely with customer success on escalations.
members.private_state: She wants a fix that can be explained cleanly to clients without reopening the broader positioning of the product; she is especially concerned about stopping false alarms in next week's executive demo and prefers changes that can be framed as validation tightening rather than model instability.
hidden_assumptions: If the burst/inter-burst duration shape looks wrong in the dashboard output, the practical problem is in the alert interpretation layer rather than the underlying simulator unless proven otherwise.
A 'memory test' means a client-safe diagnostic on the production signal stream, not a research-grade distinction between mechanistic model classes.
When the team says 'the 3/2 result,' they mean the observed slope in the operational burst-duration chart after standard smoothing and event-thresholding.
A 'fix in the pipeline' naturally includes thresholding, aggregation, and alert labeling, because clients experience these as one feature.

members.name: Ravi Menon
members.expertise: Stochastic process modeling, simulation benchmarks, statistical diagnostics for temporal dependence
members.background: Ravi has a PhD in applied probability and previously built agent-based and SDE-derived benchmark models for consumer-demand and market-microstructure products. He oversees the modeling library used to validate temporal-risk signals before release.
members.private_state: He wants to protect the scientific credibility of the team’s dependence diagnostics and is worried that the current issue comes from an implementation shortcut introduced during deployment; he prefers to isolate the problem to benchmark generation and test calibration before any dashboard-layer changes muddy the diagnosis.
hidden_assumptions: If the benchmark no longer cleanly separates Markov imitation dynamics from fractional-noise dynamics, the root cause is most likely in the simulation or test calibration, not the client-facing interpretation layer.
A 'memory test' means checking whether the estimated burst/inter-burst duration PDF reproduces the theoretically expected asymptotic behavior under controlled benchmark series.
When the team says 'the 3/2 result,' they mean the asymptotic power-law exponent from raw first-passage durations in the one-dimensional SDE benchmark.
A 'fix in the pipeline' naturally refers to the modeling and validation pipeline upstream of any dashboard thresholds or messaging.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'rerunning the memory test' as the obvious next step.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means rerunning the production diagnostic on live client-like streams to see whether the alert still tags hype episodes as persistent after normal dashboard preprocessing.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ravi means rerunning the benchmark discrimination test on synthetic series to see whether the burst/inter-burst PDFs still separate SDE-based spurious memory from fBm-like long memory under controlled conditions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In this team, 'memory test' is a familiar shorthand used across product and modeling conversations, and each person assumes the other is naturally viewing the same test through their own layer of responsibility.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both cite 'whether we still get the 3/2 result' as evidence about the root cause.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means the approximate slope visible in the dashboard’s duration-distribution panel after smoothing, bucketing, and the house event-threshold rule used in customer reports.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ravi means the asymptotic exponent estimated from raw burst or inter-burst first-passage durations in benchmark simulations before dashboard transformations.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are numerically talking about the same famous exponent from prior internal presentations, so the phrase feels highly specific and shared even though they apply it at different stages of the data pipeline.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'put in a quick fix before the client review.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena assumes the fix can include alert thresholds, burst segmentation, smoothing defaults, and the wording used in the persistence badge, because all of these jointly determine what clients see.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ravi assumes the fix is limited to the benchmark generator and the internal validation gate that approves a persistence alert model, leaving the client-facing transformations untouched for now.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'quick fix' sounds operationally aligned and appropriately temporary; since each person owns a different section of the workflow, neither feels the need to restate the boundaries of what is included.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both mention that 'this started after the last release.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena is thinking of the customer-visible release three weeks ago that changed event aggregation windows and chart smoothing on the dashboard.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ravi is thinking of the internal modeling-library release from the same week that changed numerical settings in the synthetic benchmark and default duration extraction routine.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both releases happened close together, were discussed in the same cross-functional update, and are commonly collapsed into 'the last release,' making the reference feel unambiguous when it is not.

I need this framed as an over-sensitive interpretation issue, not as the core model wobbling. If we can contain it before next week's executive demo, even better.
